lead: The weekday readings call for a decision. James gives a string of short commands to those who try to serve God and the world at once: submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, humble yourselves, and stop judging your neighbour. In Luke, Jesus says he has come to cast fire on the earth, longs for his “baptism”, the Passion, to be fulfilled, and warns that he brings division, because to follow him cuts through even the closest ties. Today the Church also remembers St Martha of Bethany, the sister of Mary and Lazarus, and gives two readings for her: the first letter of John, “God is love”, and the Gospel in which Martha, grieving for her brother, hears Jesus say, “I am the resurrection and the life”, and answers with a confession of faith. The day’s message is that love and faith ask for a whole heart, and that the one who asks for it is himself the resurrection and the life.

set: James has just spoken sharply about quarrels and cravings among Christians (4:1–6) and said that friendship with the world is enmity with God. Now he gives ten short commands, in the style of the prophets’ call to repentance. They describe one movement: turn from the devil and double-mindedness, draw near to God, and live humbly with others. The reading ends with a warning against slander and judging, which he treats as a sin against the law of love.
str: v. 7: submit to God; resist the devil and he will flee.
vv. 8–9: draw near to God; cleanse your hands and purify your hearts; lament and mourn.
v. 10: humble yourselves before the Lord and he will exalt you.
vv. 11–12: do not speak evil against one another; there is one lawgiver and judge; who are you to judge your neighbour?
kw: A military and social word for placing oneself in order under another. Before God it means a willing act of trust, not fear.
Literally “two-souled”: people who try to belong both to God and to the world. James uses the word of the one who doubts in 1:8.
In the Old Testament, priests “drew near” to God in the Temple (Exodus 19:22; Leviticus 10:3). James tells every believer to draw near, with clean hands and a pure heart, as the Psalm says (24:4).
vv: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Resistance is possible because it begins with obedience to God. The devil flees not from our strength but from our belonging to the Lord.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.
God’s nearness answers ours. The first step is a human one, yet God has long been seeking us.
Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.
It is the same promise as the Lord’s in the Gospel (Luke 14:11) and of Mary’s song (Luke 1:52). God raises the lowly.
So who, then, are you to judge your neighbor?
Only God knows hearts. When we judge, we take a place that is not ours.
ch: The Catechism teaches that humility is the foundation of prayer (CCC 2559), and that we should not judge others rashly, speak evil of them, or run down their good name (CCC 2477–2479). The Church sees in James’s call to “draw near” the movement of conversion and penance, which begins with God’s own first love for us (CCC 1427–1429). The letter’s call to resist the devil is part of the Church’s teaching that Christians are in a spiritual battle in which they can count on God’s grace (CCC 409, 2846–2849).

r.h: I came to bring fire to the earth
set: Jesus is on the way to Jerusalem (9:51), teaching his disciples and the crowds about readiness for the coming of the Son of Man (12:35–48). Then his tone turns to himself. Three short sayings speak of fire, of a baptism, and of division. They are among the hardest sayings in the Gospel because they seem to contradict the angels’ song of peace at his birth (2:14).

The fire is generally understood to mean the Holy Spirit, who will come at Pentecost (Acts 2:3), and also the purifying judgment that his coming brings. The “baptism” is his Passion (compare Mark 10:38). The “division” is the result of the choice his coming forces on each person and each household. Verse 53 echoes Micah 7:6, a prophecy of division within families before the day of the Lord.
str: v. 49: I have come to cast fire on the earth, and I wish it were already kindled.
v. 50: I have a baptism to receive, and I am under stress until it is completed.
vv. 51–53: not peace but division; households are divided, father against son, mother against daughter.
kw: In the Bible, fire is a sign of God’s presence (Exodus 3:2), of purification (Malachi 3:2–3) and of the Spirit (Acts 2:3). It does not only destroy; it refines.
From a verb meaning “to immerse”. Here it means being plunged into death, the Passion, from which Jesus will rise.
The verb means to be pressed from all sides, held in tension. It shows that Jesus approaches his Passion not with indifference but with a deep longing to complete the Father’s will.
vv: I came to bring fire to the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled!
The fire is lit by Christ’s Passion and kindled at Pentecost. He desires that it burn in every heart.
I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and what stress I am under until it is completed!
Jesus is not merely a teacher of wisdom; he goes to meet his Passion as the work for which he came.
Do you think that I have come to bring peace to the earth? No, I tell you, but rather division!
The peace he brings is real, but it is not the peace of avoiding every choice. Christ’s call asks a decision, and where people decide differently, division can come, even in homes.
ch: The Catechism teaches that fire is a symbol of the transforming energy of the Holy Spirit, and quotes this verse in speaking of the Spirit (CCC 696). It teaches that Christ’s whole life leads to his “baptism”, the Passion, which is the Father’s plan (CCC 536, 607–609). On division in families, the Catechism says that family ties are important but not absolute: a person’s vocation comes from God, and loyalty to Christ may bring misunderstanding and, at times, pain (CCC 2232–2233). The Church does not read this passage as a licence for hostility, since the same Lord commands his followers to love their enemies and to seek peace with all (Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:18). Christians are asked to remain faithful to Christ with gentleness, and to pray for those who oppose them.

set: The First Letter of John was written for a community troubled by a split in its own ranks, around the end of the first century. Its writer insists that knowing God cannot be separated from loving the brothers and sisters, and that the heart of faith is the love of God shown in the sending of his Son. This reading is given for St Martha because she is the woman of Bethany who loved the Lord and served him in her home (Luke 10:38; John 12:2).
str: vv. 7–8: love one another, for love is from God; the one who does not love does not know God, for God is love.
vv. 9–10: God’s love was shown in sending his Son; love is not that we loved God but that he loved us first.
vv. 11–12: since God has loved us, we ought to love one another; no one has seen God, but if we love, God abides in us.
vv. 13–16: the Spirit is the sign of this abiding; to confess that Jesus is the Son of God is to abide in God; God is love.
kw: The word John uses of God’s own love, without selfishness, poured out on others. To say that “God is love” is to say that God is a communion who gives himself.
The offering that removes sin and restores friendship with God. It echoes the Day of Atonement and is fulfilled in the Cross.
A favourite word in John for staying in lasting communion. God abides in us, and we in him.
vv: Whoever does not love does not know God, for God is love.
This is one of the shortest and deepest sentences in the Bible. All that we say of God must be said in the light of love.
In this is love, not that we loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
The initiative is always God’s. We love because we have first been loved.
No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God lives in us, and his love is perfected in us.
God is invisible, but the love of Christians for one another makes him visible. Love is the Church’s chief witness.
ch: The Catechism begins its teaching on the Trinity and on God with these words: God is love, and the whole life of God is a gift of himself (CCC 214, 220, 221, 257). It teaches that the Cross is the revelation of this love (CCC 604) and that the love of God and neighbour is the sum of the commandments (CCC 2055, 2196). The saints, including Martha in her service, show that loving is not a feeling but a way of life.

r.h: I am the resurrection and the life
set: Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, has died, and Jesus arrives four days later. In the Gospel, Bethany is about two miles from Jerusalem, so many from the city have come to console the sisters. John says “the Jews” here simply of these neighbours and mourners who had come to comfort the family (11:19, 31, 45). Jesus comes to a house in grief. Martha, the active sister, goes out to meet him, while Mary stays at home (compare Luke 10:38–42).

Martha’s words are a mixture of grief and faith: “If you had been here, my brother would not have died.” Yet she adds, “even now I know that God will give you whatever you ask.” Jesus answers with promise, and then with one of the great “I am” sayings of John’s Gospel. Martha’s confession that follows (11:27) is, in John, one of the clearest professions of faith: “You are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.”
str: vv. 17–20: Lazarus has been in the tomb four days; Martha goes out to meet Jesus; Mary stays at home.
vv. 21–22: Martha: if you had been here my brother would not have died; even now God will give you what you ask.
vv. 23–24: Jesus: your brother will rise again; Martha: I know he will rise at the resurrection on the last day.
vv. 25–26: Jesus: I am the resurrection and the life; those who believe in me, even though they die, will live; do you believe this?
kw: The “rising again” of the dead. Martha shares the faith of many pious Jews of the time, based on Daniel 12:2, that the dead will rise on the last day.
Jesus’ solemn way of speaking in John, echoing the divine name (Exodus 3:14). The “resurrection” is not only a future event; it is a person standing before her.
In John, not an opinion but the entrusting of oneself to Christ. “Do you believe this?” is the question to every reader.
vv: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that God will give you whatever you ask of him.
Martha’s prayer is honest. She says her pain, and she says her hope, in the same breath.
I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live
Jesus does not only promise a resurrection; he is the resurrection. Life is to be found in union with him.
Do you believe this?
A question addressed to Martha and to every Christian at a graveside. Faith is the answer of the whole person to the One who speaks.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus ties faith in the resurrection to his own person: “I am the Resurrection and the life” (CCC 994). It teaches that death is the end of earthly pilgrimage, yet for those who die in Christ it is a passage to life (CCC 1006, 1010–1014). St Augustine, preaching on the raising of Lazarus, heard in the story a call to rise from the death of sin as well as from the tomb (in substance, Tractates on John 49). The Church sees in Martha both the faithful servant and the believer who confesses Christ in the hour of loss.

qa: Who was St Martha, and is she the same as Mary Magdalene?

Martha was the sister of Mary and Lazarus, who lived at Bethany near Jerusalem and were friends of Jesus. Luke tells how she welcomed Jesus into her home and was busy with serving, and how the Lord told her gently that only one thing is needed (10:38–42). In John she confesses her faith when Lazarus dies (11:20–27), and she serves again at the supper six days before the Passover (12:2). Mary of Bethany, her sister, is not the same person as Mary Magdalene, who is a different woman from Magdala in Galilee. Martha is honoured as a model of hospitality, service and faith, and the readings of the day show that the two sides belong together: service grows from love, and love is confessed in faith.
Does Jesus really want to bring division?

Jesus does not want hatred or quarrels. He is called the Prince of Peace and gives his peace to his disciples (John 14:27). But the Gospel calls for a decision, and people in the same family may answer differently. When that happens, the Church asks believers to remain loyal to Christ with patience, love and prayer, and not to look for conflict.
study: James tells us to “draw near to God.” What is one concrete step I can take today to draw near, in prayer or in forgiveness?
Jesus says, “I came to bring fire.” Where do I feel the fire of the Spirit in my life, and where am I trying to keep it small?
Martha says her grief and her hope together to Jesus. What do I need to say to him honestly today?
